summary: The machine has the tools and DocumentDB MCP/data-plane skills needed to build and verify the sample app against the existing Azure DocumentDB cluster. Several cold answers from the model were outdated or incorrect (notably resource type naming, CLI group, capacity billing model, vector & full-text search support, Entra ID auth, and local dev ports). None of the mismatches block the build, but the builder must follow the current docs (links below). Missing CLI tools (azd, bicep, terraform) are not required; mongosh is not installed and would help manual verification. The primary information gaps are OpenAI model/dimension and the exact affinity scoring formula — the builder must choose defaults and document them.
summary_points: Everything essential to implement and verify the Beanie + async Python + OpenAI embeddings sample is present: Python, node/npx, docker, az, the documentdb MCP server, and the documentdb-* skills.

Many cold answers were outdated or wrong: the cluster resource is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), CLI group is az documentdb, billing is vCore (compute+storage) not RU-based, vector indexes and full-text search are now supported natively, and Microsoft Entra ID OIDC is supported for data-plane auth.
No required tool is missing that would block coding and verification; mongosh is absent and would make ad-hoc checks easier but is not essential.

The builder should follow the Learn docs linked below (mongoclusters, CLI, vector-search, full-text-search, auth) rather than the cold answers; several small but important differences would break the sample if used as-is.

Key information the builder must choose or confirm before coding: which OpenAI embedding model (and dimension) to use, and the exact affinity scoring formula combining co-purchase counts and vector similarity.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. The managed MongoDB cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older and different Azure services use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (classic Cosmos DB accounts) and the name overlap between 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos DB' leads to using the older resource type. The new managed MongoDB clusters use a distinct resource type 'mongoClusters'.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB - Database for the AI Era

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep templates or expects 'az cosmosdb' commands, they will fail to create/manage the vCore clusters or will target the wrong resource type (Cosmos DB accounts).
improvements: Change any quickstart/skill text that references Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for vCore clusters to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Quickstart and CLI docs).
Add a short note on the mongoClusters docs explaining the historical naming overlap with Cosmos DB and when to use mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure CLI group: az cosmosdb (subcommands like az cosmosdb create ...). This command group is part of the core az CLI.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb mongocluster command group (az documentdb mongocluster create / show / list-connection-strings). The command group is part of the documented Azure CLI (documentdb commands); it is not az cosmosdb for the vCore mongoClusters resource.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Legacy Cosmos DB CLI group 'az cosmosdb' historically managed Cosmos DB accounts; the new vCore-based managed clusters are surfaced as 'az documentdb mongocluster' and naming overlap causes mistaken memory-based answers.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB CLI docs (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands will not manage mongoClusters and will confuse automated deployment scripts; the created resources will not match the new service and may fail.
improvements: Update CLI quickstarts to show 'az documentdb mongocluster' examples prominently and mark 'az cosmosdb' as the wrong group for vCore clusters.
Add a one-line mapping in the agent skill documentation: 'for vCore Mongo clusters use az documentdb mongocluster'.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM/Terraform deployment for vCore-managed Mongo clusters uses the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (the Learn templates show the mongoClusters schema and examples). For Terraform, use AzAPI/arm templates or Azure Verified Modules for mongoClusters (not azurerm_cosmosdb_account for these vCore clusters).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: DatabaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account are the resource types for classic Cosmos DB accounts (RU model). The vCore clusters use a new resource type (mongoClusters) exposed via Microsoft.DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account in IaC will create the wrong type of resource and fail to expose the vCore cluster capabilities the sample expects.
improvements: Make the Bicep/ARM examples for mongoClusters the canonical quickstarts and add a deprecation note to older databaseAccounts examples explaining when to use each resource type.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Cosmos Mongo endpoint: mongodb://<user>:<pass>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin — scheme mongodb:// or mongodb+srv, host suffix .mongo.cosmos.azure.com, port 10255, options ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false, authSource=admin.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB managed mongoClusters typically provide SRV-style or standard Mongo connection strings like mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster-name>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 (or oauth OIDC settings) and other service-specific options. The exact host suffix and options differ from legacy cosmos endpoints (not necessarily .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255). Use the cluster's list-connection-strings output or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings to get the exact string.

grounding_links.title: Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString (PowerShell example showing SRV)
Quickstart: Connect Beanie to Azure DocumentDB (example connection string)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo endpoints used .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255. The newer vCore mongoClusters expose different hostnames (including SRV/global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and may supply SRV URIs; mixing the two leads to wrong assumptions about host suffix and port.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (legacy) connection strings

confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding the wrong host suffix/port or options can make the client fail to connect. The builder must fetch the connection string from the cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI env var per run notes or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings) rather than hardcoding legacy Cosmos connection options.
improvements: In quickstarts and the agent kit, show the recommended pattern: always use az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or the portal copy-to-clipboard value and avoid reusing legacy cosmos connection examples.
Add an example SRV-based and a non-SRV connection string in the Beanie quickstart and mark which parameters (tls/authMechanism) are required.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Provisioning/billing is primarily RU-based: provisioned throughput measured in Request Units per second (RU/s). There is also serverless option and dedicated cluster SKUs (vCore).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore-managed managed Mongo offering) is billed by compute tier (vCores) and storage (per-GiB). It is *not* RU-based. The vCore + storage billing model is the primary billing model for Azure DocumentDB clusters (compute tiers like M30, M40 etc.).

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Compute and storage configurations for Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Azure Cosmos DB's RU billing model is prominent and the older Cosmos Mongo API used RU throughput; the vCore-based DocumentDB offering uses vCore+storage which is different. The common 'Cosmos' memory causes cross-wiring.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB Request Units (RU) docs

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based throughput, they might design a sample that tries to set RU targets or rely on RU metrics; that will not match vCore clusters and will misdocument cost/scale guidance.
improvements: Document clearly in the quickstart and agent kit that vCore+storage is the billing model for Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters and show the compute tier examples (M30 etc.).
Add a short note in migration docs explaining differences between RU-mode Cosmos accounts and vCore DocumentDB clusters.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Mostly username/password (SCRAM). Azure AD support unclear; direct Azure AD authentication for MongoDB drivers not generally supported historically.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication for data plane. Microsoft Entra ID is implemented via OpenID Connect (OIDC); clients present an Entra-issued OIDC access token and can use connection strings with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC or include the token in driver APIs that accept access tokens. Clusters can enable NativeAuth, MicrosoftEntraID, or both.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older or different Cosmos DB variants exposed limited Entra ID support; the newer vCore DocumentDB clusters explicitly added Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) support for data-plane auth and the docs show authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC examples.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only username/password is available, they may not design for managed identities or Entra-based flows; if Entra auth is required by the cluster admin, the sample might fail to authenticate.
improvements: Add an explicit section in the connection/driver skill and quickstarts showing both native SCRAM and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) connection examples including connection string parameters (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo/motor), use Beanie ODM on top of motor/pymongo; avoid Cosmos-specific SDK when using Mongo compatibility.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Use standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo / Motor / AsyncMongoClient). Beanie (ODM) sits on top of the Mongo driver and is an appropriate choice for an async Python sample. The Learn quickstarts for DocumentDB show Beanie + PyMongo/AsyncMongoClient examples.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Beanie to Azure DocumentDB
Frequently asked questions: Are MongoDB drivers and tools compatible with Azure DocumentDB?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB / DocumentDB did not support built-in vector indexes; no createIndex for vectors.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect. Azure DocumentDB now provides integrated vector indexes. Supported kinds include vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann. You create them via db.runCommand({ createIndexes: '<coll>', indexes: [ { name: '...', key: { '<path>':'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann', dimensions: N, similarity: 'COS'|'L2'|'IP', ... } } ] }) or via the documentdb/create_index API. The Learn docs supply full parameter examples for each algorithm.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Vector search examples and create-index
LangChain / LangChain-Azure vector index examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Vector search was added later and older memory/notes for Cosmos DB lacked integrated vector indexes; the model recalled older limits. Vector-index support is a relatively new capability.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no native vector index, they might store embeddings but not create the appropriate vector index, leading to slow or missing kNN queries. Use the documented cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions syntax to create a vector index with the right dimensions.
improvements: Add a short index-creation example to the Beanie quickstart showing cosmosSearch vector indexing and include example cosmosSearchOptions for HNSW and DiskANN.
Document the mapping between OpenAI model dims and 'dimensions' used in createIndex examples.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search / Azure Search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Outdated. Azure DocumentDB exposes a built-in full-text search engine (createSearchIndexes + $search) with BM25 ranking and supports hybrid keyword + vector retrieval (BM25 + vector) fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). You enable full-text search on the cluster and create search indexes with createSearchIndexes; hybrid queries combine $search (BM25) and cosmosSearch vector queries and fuse results.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many Cosmos DB scenarios historically used Azure Cognitive Search for rich text search; the newer integrated search engine in DocumentDB is recent and the model reflected older practices.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder pipelines vector search into Azure Cognitive Search instead of using the integrated engine, they'll create unnecessary ETL and complexity; sample should use integrated $search + cosmosSearch unless the user prefers Cognitive Search.
improvements: Update high-level migration and quickstart docs to call out the integrated full-text engine and how it differs from Azure Cognitive Search to avoid recommending an external search service by default.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically supported versions 3.x/4.x; many features missing; assume 4.x compatibility.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (current docs list support through 8.0). Most MongoDB drivers and standard aggregation stages/operators are supported; there remain a small number of unsupported admin commands and a few operator-level differences documented on the compatibility page. Check the compatibility matrix to confirm operator/stage support for your workload.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance - MongoDB compatibility summary

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Model memory was outdated; supported protocol versions have been expanded. The product supports more recent Mongo wire protocol versions than the cold answer assumed.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming older protocol versions could cause the builder to pin an unnecessarily old driver or avoid newer language features; check the cluster's 'serverVersion' and use compatible driver versions as recommended in quickstarts.
improvements: Add a prominent compatibility matrix link to quickstarts showing supported wire protocol versions and the recommended driver versions to use.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for SQL endpoint; emulator historically does not support Mongo API, so must test cloud; TLS port 10255 for cloud.
confusions.grounded_answer: For local development, use the open-source DocumentDB gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) which exposes the gateway on port 10260 by default (connection example: mongodb://<user>:<pass>@localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true). The Azure Cosmos DB emulator is a separate product and does not fully cover the vCore DocumentDB Mongo API. For the cloud cluster, use the connection string from the portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings (SRV host or TLS endpoints).

grounding_links.title: Run DocumentDB in Docker (development loop)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB emulator covers SQL API scenarios; the open-source DocumentDB gateway is the correct local dev tooling for the DocumentDB engine and uses a different port (10260).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes there's no local image and writes tests that require a live cloud cluster, test iteration becomes slower. The local DocumentDB image on 10260 can speed development.
improvements: Add a short 'Local dev' section to the quickstart showing docker run with port 10260 and the exact TLS connection example for developers.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams were not historically supported; Cosmos offers change feed on SQL API; Mongo change streams likely not supported.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB. The docs include examples and mention enabling change stream feature where required for migration scenarios. You can open a change stream via db.collection.watch() and resume using resume tokens. For online migration and other use-cases, enable and configure change streams per the docs.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Migrate from Amazon DocumentDB to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) - online migration uses change streams

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Change-stream-like features historically differed between Cosmos APIs and older Mongo offers; the model recalled older limitations. The vCore DocumentDB product now supports change streams and uses them in migration tooling.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are not available, they might implement inefficient polling or avoid implementing incremental/upstream sync/migration flows.
improvements: Document change-stream enablement steps in the migration quickstart and show a code example for Python or Node showing db.collection.watch() and resume token usage.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server for DocumentDB/Cosmos DB-specific data-plane tooling; azure MCP covers control-plane.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, aggregate, explain, etc.) and should be used for collection/index/query inspection. The general azure MCP server is useful for control-plane management but not for data-plane operations.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Originally called DocumentDB, later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB; Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is proprietary; unrelated to open-source DocumentDB project.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong / misleading. History is nuanced: the original Microsoft 'DocumentDB' (2014–2017) evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. Separately, the open-source project named DocumentDB powers the new vCore managed offering now called Azure DocumentDB (previously 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'); Microsoft reintroduced the 'DocumentDB' product name for the vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible service. Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is distinct from Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) and from AWS Amazon DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: FAQ: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB?
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? Naming and history

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The name 'DocumentDB' was used historically and is now used again for a distinct vCore product; overlapping names and rebranding create confusion between old DocumentDB, Cosmos DB, and the new DocumentDB product built on the open-source engine.
confusions.build_risk: Documentation or README that uses the wrong name may confuse users, pointing them at the wrong CLI, resource type, or migration path (RU-based Cosmos vs vCore DocumentDB).
improvements: Add a short 'Naming' section to the quickstart and readme explaining: (a) the historical DocumentDB → Cosmos rename, (b) the new Azure DocumentDB (vCore) product relationship to the open-source engine, and (c) how it differs from Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU).

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underlying engine is Cosmos DB proprietary storage with Mongo wire protocol; code mostly works but watch for feature gaps.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation) which implements the MongoDB wire protocol. Applications using standard MongoDB drivers typically work, but builders must check the compatibility matrix for specific operators/commands. The engine being different from MongoDB server means some administrative commands or server-specific extensions are not available; testing is required.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated older Cosmos internals with the new open-source DocumentDB engine. The practical guidance (use Mongo drivers and test) is correct, but the engine identity matters for licensing and behavior.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the actual MongoDB server engine, they might use unsupported admin commands or expect some server-specific behaviour that DocumentDB does not provide.
improvements: Add an explicit 'engine & compatibility' paragraph in quickstarts clarifying that DocumentDB uses the DocumentDB open-source engine and listing practical differences to watch for.

confusions.question: Which database name and environment variable will the sample use to connect at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Database name: sample_retail_19. Read the connection URI from environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the run-environment notes specify using DATABASE 'sample_retail_19' and reading the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime; do not write secrets to source control.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Beanie to Azure DocumentDB (example .env and usage)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What exact Mongo connection string options should the sample include when building the Motor/Beanie client?
confusions.cold_answer: Use TLS and Cosmos-specific options: include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false, authSource=admin, example: mongodb://...:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong. For modern DocumentDB mongoclusters the connection string commonly uses SRV-style hostnames (mongodb+srv://...) or cluster-provided strings; required options include TLS (tls=true or tls=true in SRV), and the proper authMechanism (SCRAM-SHA-256 for native, or MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID). The legacy replicaSet=globaldb and the 10255 port are specific to older Cosmos DB endpoints; the builder must use the exact connection string returned by the cluster (or via az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings) rather than hardcoding legacy Cosmos options.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Beanie to Azure DocumentDB (connection string example)
Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString (PowerShell example SRV)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Legacy Cosmos DB connection strings used replicaSet=globaldb and a fixed TLS port; the new mongoClusters often provide SRV URIs and different hostnames.
confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding legacy options could fail TLS/host resolution or pick wrong auth mechanisms. The builder must accept DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it into AsyncIOMotorClient (or AsyncMongoClient) unchanged and only add minimal options if needed.
improvements: Document in quickstarts: 'Do not modify the cluster-provided connection string; copy it from the portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings.'
Show both SRV and non-SRV connection examples and show how to pass the DOCUMENTDB_URI into Motor/Beanie initialization.

confusions.question: What vector index definition will the sample expect to create for storing embeddings (index name, field, algorithm, dims, metric)?
confusions.cold_answer: Assuming vector index support exists, create a vector index on 'pair_embedding' with HNSW algorithm and cosine distance; example createIndex with cosmosSearchOptions kind: 'hnsw' dims 1536 metric 'cosine'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Mostly correct in spirit. The concrete syntax uses cosmosSearchOptions with kind: 'vector-hnsw' | 'vector-ivf' | 'vector-diskann' and fields like dimensions, similarity (COS, L2, IP), and algorithm parameters (m/efConstruction for HNSW, numLists for IVF, lBuild/lSearch etc for DiskANN). The dimension must match the chosen embedding model (e.g., 1536 for text-embedding-3-small). Use the documented createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions examples.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB - example and options
Perform vector similarity search and DiskANN/HNSW/IVF guidance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer's structure is OK but used a shorthand that didn't match the exact parameter names (kind 'vector-hnsw' vs 'hnsw'), and dimension depends on the embedding model choice.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder picks the wrong dimension, index creation will succeed but search results will be invalid or the index will reject documents. The builder must align embedding model dims and the vector index dimensions.
improvements: Add a small table in the vector-search docs mapping common embedding models (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, etc.) to index 'dimensions' and recommended index kind for sample sizes.

confusions.question: How will the Python Beanie app connect and initialise models (exact code lines to create client and init Beanie)?
confusions.cold_answer: Use AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']); db = client.get_database('sample_retail_19'); await init_beanie(database=db, document_models=[Order, ProductPairEmbedding])
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: The Beanie quickstart shows the same pattern. Use one Async client per process, pass the database object to init_beanie with the document models list. Ensure correct driver/client version (Beanie 2 and PyMongo / AsyncMongoClient or Beanie 2.2 + PyMongo 4.19 in the quickstart).

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: Which port should the sample assume for TLS connections to the managed cluster and what port would a dev use for a local emulator (if available)?
confusions.cold_answer: Assume TLS port 10255 for the managed MongoDB-compatible cluster. For the Cosmos DB emulator the management endpoint is https://localhost:8081 but emulator historically doesn't expose a fully compatible Mongo TLS port; tests should target the live cluster on 10255.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong. For local DocumentDB development the gateway Docker image exposes port 10260 (development-loop docs). For managed clusters the service commonly provides SRV connection strings (mongodb+srv) or TLS endpoints — do not assume port 10255 (legacy Cosmos). Always use the connection string returned for the cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) rather than a hardcoded port.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Port 10255 is associated with older Cosmos DB Mongo endpoints; the new DocumentDB local gateway uses 10260. Cloud clusters may not expose that exact port and often use SRV records.
confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding the wrong port will break connections; the builder must use DOCUMENTDB_URI or the cluster-provided connection strings.
improvements: Update quickstarts to show both: (a) how to read the cluster connection string (az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings), and (b) how to run the local Docker gateway on 10260 for dev/testing.

The builder must pick a model (e.g., text-embedding-3-small with 1536 dims) or ask the author. I checked the prompt and quickstart docs; none specified the embedding model or env var name for OpenAI.

information_gaps.title: Affinity scoring formula
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires ranking candidates by 'affinity score' combining co-purchase counts and vector similarity, but no canonical formula is provided. No skill or doc prescribes a specific combination formula; the builder must choose and document a heuristic (e.g., normalize co-purchase counts and average cosine similarities across basket items, then weighted sum).

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset specifics
information_gaps.description: The prompt left the sample data unspecified (size, field names, distribution). The documentdb-local-deployment skill suggests using a synthetic generator but does not give a specific sample dataset. The builder must choose or request a seed dataset size and format.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create and manage clusters (IaC or CLI) using the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource and the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group; do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb for vCore mongo clusters.

sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Do not assume RU-based billing. Treat Azure DocumentDB clusters as vCore + storage billed services (tiers like M30); design the sample's guidance and README accordingly.

Use the connection string provided by the cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime; do not hardcode legacy cosmos options like replicaSet=globaldb or port 10255. If you need Microsoft Entra ID auth, use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and obtain an OIDC token per the DocumentDB docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: azd (Azure Developer CLI) is not required for this sample; the builder can use az and Bicep or local scripts instead. Do not add unless you plan to include azd deployment automation.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is only needed if the sample includes in-repo IaC the builder will run locally. The sample can include ARM/Bicep templates but not execute them; if you want to run IaC locally, install bicep (`az bicep install`) or use az deployment commands as a fallback.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform is unnecessary for building the sample application itself. If the team wants IaC with Terraform, add AzAPI provider examples and install terraform; otherwise document how to verify using az and the documentdb MCP server.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: dotnet is not required for this Python sample; skip installing unless adding .NET examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on the dev machine (recommended) to run quick ad-hoc checks and index/list operations against the cluster or the local DocumentDB Docker gateway. Install from MongoDB download pages or via package manager.
